I'm now writing the explainer HTML, which will be a large file, so I want to design it carefully. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 logical canvas scaled to fit the window, with letterboxing in the background color. Inside it, I'm planning a left rail with numbered chapter items and a top bar carrying the "Moneo · Artifacts deep dive" eyebrow and a progress indicator.

I'm sketching out the scene list and the interaction model next. Navigation will work with the arrow keys, Space, Home and End, plus a dark-mode toggle and fullscreen, and clicking a rail item jumps straight to that chapter. For the shared styling I'm defining the eyebrow labels, display headings, white cards, and colour-coded diagram nodes, and I'll place the architecture diagram with absolute positioning inside the fixed stage so an SVG can draw the connecting paths.

I'm sketching out the scenes next, starting with a title slide that pairs the "Artifacts" headline with example floating cards, and then a "What it is" slide laying out the three parts: the ask, the page, and the home cards. The "hard part" slide will list five constraints, covering correctness, privacy, safety, staying current, and looking native.

I'm now laying out the architecture diagram as two lanes: build time on top and view time below. The top lane runs from the owner's prompt through the artifact chat and designer model, past a verify gate, and into Postgres, which stores only code and queries, never data. The bottom lane starts from Postgres, goes through the query runner, and then splits into a page path and a card path.

Next I'm sketching the data contract scene: a simplified saved query on the left, with the period set to relative tokens, and a timeline on the right showing when it was opened.

I'm now working out the data contract scene: the saved query's period uses relative tokens, so the same query resolves to a new month each time the page is opened. Literal dates are refused unless fixedDates is set, and money values stay as integer strings that become BigInt rather than being parsed from formatted text. The model writes the presentation, while the app owns the numbers. Then I'm sketching the generate-and-verify loop, where failed checks feed their errors back into the prompt for up to three retries before saving a new version.

Next I'm covering how the card checks work: the compiled code runs at all four sizes with today's data, the sliders are tested at their minimum and maximum with the switches flipped, and every declared parameter must have a matching control. The durability side runs the generation through a database row and a background task, so it keeps going if the tab closes, and it re-checks that the run is still active right before saving so a cancelled run never writes a version.

Now I'm turning to the page sandbox, which I'm drawing as nested boxes: the Moneo app wraps an iframe that loads the frame route, and that route sends back a strict content security policy and a sandbox attribute.

I'm now working through the security section, listing the ways the sandboxed page could try to get out, like network requests, image URLs, form submissions, navigation, cookies, and external scripts, and noting how each one gets blocked.

I'm now moving on to the cards section, explaining why I'm not using a separate iframe for each card. Each card's code returns data rather than DOM, and I'm sketching the pipeline from the designer's TSX through the sandboxed runtime to Moneo's own React components. Next I'm listing the allowlist that the tree check will enforce.

Now I'm listing the allowed HTML and SVG elements and attributes, banning href and src, and limiting url(#id) references to scoped ones. CSS gets rewritten under a scoped attribute selector, with imports, url() calls, and backslash escapes removed, and keyframes and ids namespaced. On the card side, the Kit props are validated strictly, and I'm planning the second path for interactivity: month changes re-fetch the card from the server, while sliders and toggles run locally.

I'm covering the speed side next: the cache key includes the data, so cached results can't go stale, and cards on Home share their query results so each query runs only once. I'm also making sure one failing card shows its own error message instead of breaking the whole page. Then I'm looking at history and control: versions are append-only, drafts stay out of the Home view, and adding, updating, or removing cards from Home is always the owner's action.

I'm laying out the decisions table next, with each choice paired against the alternative it replaces and the reason behind it. The first rows cover saving queries instead of baked numbers, the two-model split, and verifying before saving, and I'm about to add the double sandboxed iframe and the JSON-tree cards drawn by our own React components.

Now I'm working through the remaining decisions in the table: choosing QuickJS over node:vm, eval, or a Web Worker for real isolation with memory and time limits, and adding an allowlist tree check after the sandbox since the sandbox alone doesn't stop markup or CSS from leaking data. I'm placing the screen node and the card branch in the bottom lane, with the query runner anchored under Postgres at the right so its paths run back left to the page and the cards.

Moneo · open-source personal finance · deep dive

Artifacts

Pages and Home cards an AI builds from your real finances, and how Moneo runs AI-written code without trusting it.

Page

Subscription radar

4 schedules · yearly estimate

Illustrative numbers

The feature

One chat. One page. Any number of Home cards.

An artifact is a small app built from your data. You describe it, Moneo builds it, and it refreshes every time you open it.

1 · Ask

Describe it

“Show my Scalable portfolio with an allocation donut.” The artifact gets its own chat with every normal chat tool, the mic and cancel.

The chat reads your data with the same read-only tools as Moneo's assistant, then hands a brief to a designer model.
2 · Page

A full interactive page

HTML, CSS and JavaScript written by the model: charts, tables, what-if sliders. It runs in a sandbox that can't reach the network.

  • ECharts, served by Moneo itself
  • Moneo's colours, light and dark
  • Every version kept
3 · Home cards

Widgets that look native

Any part of it becomes a card on Home, in four sizes. You preview a draft, then add it yourself. Moneo's own React draws it, so it's not an iframe.

  • S · M · L · XL, checked at each size
  • Month switches, sliders, toggles
  • Sits next to the built-in widgets

The model writes the design. Every number comes from the app.

The problem

AI-written code, next to your money

Generating a pretty page is easy. Five things make it hard to do responsibly:

Correct

Numbers can't be guessed

Money is integer minor units with a currency. The model must never type an amount.

Current

Open it next month

It should show next month's numbers, not a snapshot from the day it was built.

Safe

Treat the code as hostile

The model reads your merchants and notes. A prompt injection in a transaction could steer it.

Private

Local-first

Moneo runs on 127.0.0.1. A generated page must have no way to send your data anywhere.

Native

Feels like the app

A Home card should look like Moneo built it, not like an embedded web page.

Each of these became one layer of the architecture. Here's how they fit together.

Layer 2 · Never save something broken

Two models, and a gate between them and your Home

Chat model

Durable

Layer 4 · Native: Home cards

A card's code returns JSON. Moneo draws it.

Ten iframes on Home would be slow, can't share Moneo's components or theme, and never quite look native. So a card isn't a web page.

// written by the designer model
export default function Card({ data, params, size }) {
  const extra = BigInt(params.extra);
  const total = BigInt(data.saved.net_minor) + extra * 60n;
  return <div>
    <Kit.Money minor={total.toString()} currency="EUR" />
    <Kit.Param name="extra" />
    {size !== "S" && <Kit.Chart type="area" … />}
  </div>;
}
// what leaves the sandbox: plain data
{ "type": "div", "props": {}, "children": [
  { "type": "kit:Money",
    "props": { "minor": "4190000", "currency": "EUR" } },
  { "type": "kit:Param", "props": { "name": "extra" } },
  { "type": "kit:Chart", … }
]}
// Kit is a Proxy: Kit.Money is just the string "kit:Money"

Layer 4 · Defence in depth

The sandbox stops code. The check stops markup.

QuickJS can't touch the host, but the tree it returns is still untrusted: a stray url() in CSS is a request. So every node is checked before React sees it.

Elements

Allowlisted HTML and SVG

  • div, table, progress, svg, path, gradients, filters…
  • No a, img, script, form, iframe or <use>
  • No event handlers
Attributes & CSS

Nothing that loads

  • Only url(#local-id), rewritten to the card's scope
  • url(), image-set(), @import refused; backslashes refused so escapes can't spell them
  • CSS parsed with PostCSS, every selector prefixed with the card, keyframes renamed
Kit

The only interactive parts

  • Money, Chart, Tabs, Param, Link, Style
  • Props parsed with Zod .strict(); unknown props refused
  • Kit.Link only goes to Moneo's own pages, by enum

Errors aren't silent: they go back to the designer, which fixes the card before it's ever saved.

Interactivity

New data goes to the server. A what-if stays in your browser.

Month switch · period · choice

Needs different data

Click “October”

→

GET /api/cards/:id
?p.month=2026-10

→

queries · QuickJS · check

The param resolves into the saved query's dates on the server. Older responses that arrive late are ignored.

Slider · toggle

Same data, new maths

Drag to €350

→

QuickJS WASM, loaded in the browser on demand

→

same tree check · zero requests

The server sends the compiled code and data along with the card. The browser reruns it in the same sandbox, so it responds instantly.

One engine, one check, on both sides of the wire.

Performance

A sandbox on every render, and Home still feels instant

Cache

Keyed by the data itself

sha256([renderer, workspace,
  cardVersion, { data, params, size }])

Same inputs, same tree, so a repeat view skips the sandbox. The data is in the key, so a cached card is never older than its data. 500-entry LRU.

Shared reads

One query, many cards

Cards on one Home share a promise map, so five cards that need balances run that read once.

Streaming

Each card on its own

Every card is its own Suspense boundary. A slow Scalable call delays one card, and an error becomes a message in that card instead of a broken Home.

Ownership

The AI proposes. You publish.

Moneo keeps the history of anything that touches your money. Artifacts follow the same rule.

Versions

Append-only

Every page and card change is a new row in artifact_versions or artifact_card_versions. Nothing is edited in place.

Draft → Home

Your button, not the model's

A new card is a draft you preview at each size. published_version only moves when you press Add or Update, and Home never shows a draft's title.

Reverse path

Clean exits

Remove a card, delete an artifact, reset all data: they drop off Home and are covered by the workspace reset and isolation tests.

Decisions

What I chose, and why

ChoseInstead ofBecause
Save queries, rerun on viewBake data into HTMLPages stay current, and every number is app-made
Chat model + designer modelOne model does it allThe planner keeps tools and history; the designer gets a focused brief and a real data sample
Verify, retry with errors, then saveSave and hopeA broken version never replaces a working one
Two sandboxed frames + CSPOne iframeOnly the parent's frame-src can stop the page navigating out with data
Cards as a JSON tree, drawn by our ReactAn iframe per cardNative look, one theme, cheap to have many on Home
QuickJS in WASMeval, node:vm, Web WorkerReal isolation with memory and time limits, and the same engine on server and browser
ECharts from Moneo's node_modulesA CDNWorks offline, and the CSP can forbid every other origin

Takeaway

Let the model design.
Let the app own the truth.

Numbers from code

Saved queries, rerun every view.

Code that can't leak

CSP, sandboxed frames, QuickJS, an allowlist.

Owner in control

Verified versions, drafts, your publish button.

The feature

One chat. One page. Any number of Home cards.

An artifact is a small app built from your data. You describe it, Moneo builds it, and it refreshes every time you open it.

1 · Ask

Describe it

“Show my Scalable portfolio with an allocation donut.” The artifact gets its own chat with every normal chat tool, the mic and cancel.

The chat reads your data with the same read-only tools as Moneo's assistant, then hands a brief to a designer model.
2 · Page

A full interactive page

HTML, CSS and JavaScript written by the model: charts, tables, what-if sliders. It runs in a sandbox that can't reach the network.

  • ECharts, served by Moneo itself
  • Moneo's colours, light and dark
  • Every version kept
3 · Home cards

Widgets that look native

Any part of it becomes a card on Home, in four sizes. You preview a draft, then add it yourself. Moneo's own React draws it, so it's not an iframe.

  • S · M · L · XL, checked at each size
  • Month switches, sliders, toggles
  • Sits next to the built-in widgets

The model writes the design. Every number comes from the app.

The problem

AI-written code, next to your money

Generating a pretty page is easy. Five things make it hard to do responsibly:

Correct

Numbers can't be guessed

Money is integer minor units with a currency. The model must never type an amount.

Current

Open it next month

It should show next month's numbers, not a snapshot from the day it was built.

Safe

Treat the code as hostile

The model reads your merchants and notes. A prompt injection in a transaction could steer it.

Private

Local-first

Moneo runs on 127.0.0.1. A generated page must have no way to send your data anywhere.

Native

Feels like the app

A Home card should look like Moneo built it, not like an embedded web page.

Each of these became one layer of the architecture. Here's how they fit together.

// written by the designer model
export default function Card({ data, params, size }) {
  const extra = BigInt(params.extra);
  const total = BigInt(data.saved.net_minor) + extra * 60n;
  return <div>
    <Kit.Money minor={total.toString()} currency="EUR" />
    <Kit.Param name="extra" />
    {size !== "S" && <Kit.Chart type="area" … />}
  </div>;
}
// what leaves the sandbox: plain data
{ "type": "div", "props": {}, "children": [
  { "type": "kit:Money",
    "props": { "minor": "4190000", "currency": "EUR" } },
  { "type": "kit:Param", "props": { "name": "extra" } },
  { "type": "kit:Chart", … }
]}
// Kit is a Proxy: Kit.Money is just the string "kit:Money"

Layer 4 · Defence in depth

The sandbox stops code. The check stops markup.

QuickJS can't touch the host, but the tree it returns is still untrusted: a stray url() in CSS is a request. So every node is checked before React sees it.

Elements

Allowlisted HTML and SVG

  • div, table, progress, svg, path, gradients, filters…
  • No a, img, script, form, iframe or <use>
  • No event handlers
Attributes & CSS

Nothing that loads

  • Only url(#local-id), rewritten to the card's scope
  • url(), image-set(), @import refused; backslashes refused so escapes can't spell them
  • CSS parsed with PostCSS, every selector prefixed with the card, keyframes renamed
Kit

The only interactive parts

  • Money, Chart, Tabs, Param, Link, Style
  • Props parsed with Zod .strict(); unknown props refused
  • Kit.Link only goes to Moneo's own pages, by enum

Errors aren't silent: they go back to the designer, which fixes the card before it's ever saved.

Nov 7, 2026, 10:18 PM

Build a savings what-if page: from my income and spending over the last 6 months, show what I save on average each month, then a slider for how much extra I could save per month (EUR 0 to 1,000) and a horizon slider (1 to 10 years), with a chart of where my savings would be over time, with and without the extra, and a switch for a 5% yearly return. Moneo's look, light and dark, phone-friendly. Then make a medium Home card with the extra-savings slider and the return switch that shows the projected amount in 5 years and a small area chart, recalculating instantly as the slider moves.

Nov 7, 2026, 10:18 PM

Moneo

Used 4 tools

The savings what-if page is built, with the extra-savings and horizon sliders, optional 5% return, and a projection chart. The medium Home card is ready as a draft in the Home card tab; you can add it to Home there.

The projection is an estimate based on the last six months’ monthly net, starts from zero, and excludes existing balances. Source coverage may be incomplete, so it may not reflect all your finances.

input.content:
# Moneo Artifacts: video script

A deep dive of about 9½ minutes for technical viewers and recruiters. You on camera, plus screen recording.

- **Screen A** is Moneo running at `http://localhost:3000`.
- **Screen B** is `docs/artifacts-deep-dive.html`, opened in a browser and full screen with `F`. Press `→` or click to reveal the next step. `←` steps back, `D` switches light and dark, and `R` hides the chapter rail. The scene numbers below match the rail.

Delivery: talk to one engineer you respect, not to a crowd. Short sentences, and pause after each reveal. Never read the slide aloud; say *why* it's there. The lines below are a guide, so say them in your own words.

---

## Before you record

- [ ] Home shows the three artifact cards: **Subscription radar**, **Scalable portfolio** and **Savings what-if**.
- [ ] Have one artifact chat ready to type into, so the opening shows a live build. The Savings what-if chat works: ask it for something small, like "add a line for a 3% return".
- [ ] Open the explainer in a second window or tab, already on scene 1.
- [ ] Close notifications. Zoom the browser to about 110% so text reads on YouTube.
- [ ] Your real balances and positions will be on screen. That's your choice; check nothing else in the sidebar or tabs is private.

---

## 0:00 – 1:00 · Cold open: the demo (Screen A)

**[Start on Moneo's Home, cards visible.]**

> This is Moneo, an open-source personal-finance app I built that runs on your own computer.
>
> Everything on this Home looks like part of the app. But three of these cards didn't exist in the code yesterday. This subscription radar, this Scalable portfolio card, this savings slider: I asked for them in plain English, and Moneo built them from my real data.

**[Drag the savings slider. The number and chart move instantly.]**

> That's not a screenshot. It's live. Drag it and it recalculates instantly, without a network request.

**[Click into the Scalable portfolio card → open its full page.]**

> Behind each card is a full page: charts, tables, my actual positions. Open it next month and it shows next month's numbers.

**[Go to the artifact chat, type a small change, press Enter. Let it build in the background.]**

> And you change it by asking. This runs on the server, so if I close this tab, it keeps going.

**[Back to Home.]**

> So: AI writes code that runs next to my bank data, and it looks like I wrote it. In the next eight minutes I'll show you how that works without trusting the AI with a single number, or with a single byte leaving this machine.

---

## 1:00 – 1:30 · Scenes 1–2: what an artifact is (Screen B)

**[Scene 1, title. Pause one beat.]**

> I call these artifacts. Quick stack: Next.js 16, React 19, Postgres, the Vercel AI SDK, and a JavaScript engine compiled to WebAssembly called QuickJS. You'll see why that last one matters.

**[Scene 2. → → → →]**

> An artifact is one chat, one full page, and any number of Home cards.
> **[→]** You describe it. The chat has the same read-only tools as Moneo's assistant.
> **[→]** It produces a page, real HTML and JavaScript…
> **[→]** …and cards that sit on Home next to the built-in widgets.
> **[→]** And the one rule behind all of it: the model writes the design, and the app supplies every number.

---

## 1:30 – 2:15 · Scene 3: why this is hard

> Generating a nice-looking page is the easy part. Doing it responsibly next to someone's money is hard for five reasons.

**[→ one per sentence]**

> **Correct:** money here is integer cents with a currency, and a model must never type an amount.
> **Current:** a page built today has to be right next month.
> **Safe:** the model reads my merchant names and notes, so text in a transaction could try to steer it. I treat everything it writes as hostile code.
> **Private:** Moneo is local-first. A generated page must have *no* path to send my data anywhere.
> **Native:** it has to feel like the app, not an iframe from 2009.

**[→ tagline]**

> Each of these became one layer of the architecture.

---

## 2:15 – 3:30 · Scene 4: architecture

> Two halves. The top half runs once, when you ask for a change. The bottom half runs every time you open it.

**[→ step 1]**

> I ask in the artifact's chat. The chat model reads my data with normal tools, then calls one of four tools: write a page, write a card, use a preset card, or remove a card.

**[→ step 2]**

> It doesn't write the code itself. It writes a *brief* with exact field paths, and a second model, the designer, writes the HTML or the React. The designer also gets a real sample of the data, so it designs for the true shape instead of guessing.

**[→ step 3]**

> Then there's a gate. The output has to parse, compile and render at every size with real data. If it fails, the errors go back to the designer, up to three tries. Nothing broken is ever saved.

**[→ step 4]**

> What gets saved is the code and the *queries*, as append-only versions. Never the numbers.

**[→ step 5]**

> Now the bottom half. Every time you open it, the query runner turns those saved queries into fresh data, with the same finance code as the rest of Moneo.

**[→ step 6]**

> A page goes into a double-sandboxed iframe…

**[→ step 7]**

**[→]**

- [ ] Open the explainer in a second window or tab, already on scene 1.
- [ ] Close notifications. Zoom the browser to about 110% so text reads on YouTube.
- [ ] Your real balances and positions will be on screen. That's your choice; check nothing else in the sidebar or tabs is private.

---

**[Start on Moneo's Home, cards visible.]**

> This is Moneo, an open-source personal-finance app I built that runs on your own computer.
>
> Everything on this Home looks like part of the app. But three of these cards didn't exist in the code yesterday. This subscription radar, this Scalable portfolio card, this savings slider: I asked for them in plain English, and Moneo built them from my real data.

**[Drag the savings slider. The number and chart move instantly.]**

> That's not a screenshot. It's live. Drag it and it recalculates instantly, without a network request.

**[Click into the Scalable portfolio card → open its full page.]**

> Behind each card is a full page: charts, tables, my actual positions. Open it next month and it shows next month's numbers.

**[Go to the artifact chat, type a small change, press Enter. Let it build in the background.]**

> And you change it by asking. This runs on the server, so if I close this tab, it keeps going.

**[Back to Home.]**

> So: AI writes code that runs next to my bank data, and it looks like I wrote it. In the next eight minutes I'll show you how that works without trusting the AI with a single number, or with a single byte leaving this machine.

> **[→]** You describe it. The chat has the same read-only tools as Moneo's assistant.

> Each of these became one layer of the architecture.

**[→ step 1]**

> A page goes into a double-sandboxed iframe…

> So the model runs once, and the data runs every time. That one idea solves *correct* and *current*.

7 Nov 2026, 10:16 pm

Build a page about my Scalable Capital portfolio: the total value and overall gain up top, an allocation donut by position (ECharts), a table of every position with shares, value, cost, gain and gain %, sorted by value, and my recent Scalable activity. Use Moneo's own look, calm and big figures, and make it work in light and dark and on a phone. Then also make a medium Home card with the portfolio total, the overall gain and a small allocation donut.

7 Nov 2026, 10:17 pm

Moneo

Used 4 tools

Done. The portfolio page is built with the total value, all-time gain, position allocation, sorted positions table, and recent activity. I also created a medium Home card draft with the portfolio total, all-time gain, and position allocation donut. The card is in the Home card tab for you to add to Home.

7 Nov 2026, 10:20 pm

The Home card's layout breaks at M: the total is cut off to "E…" and the donut legend is squeezed into a thin column. Redesign the card: on the left, the portfolio total big on one line with the all-time gain under it (red if negative) and a small securities / cash / crypto split; on the right, a compact donut with at most the top 3 positions as a short legend (names truncated with an ellipsis, value right-aligned). At S show only the total and the gain. At L and XL also add a slim list of all positions. Nothing may overflow at any size.

7 Nov 2026, 10:21 pm

Redesigned the Scalable portfolio card with the responsive layouts you described. The new version is a draft in the Home card tab; preview it there, then add or update it on Home.
